To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
seasonal and episodic precipitation inputs drive soil respi- ration (SR) dynamics and the contributions of root versus microbial sources to SR in semi-arid and arid eco- systems.

1) soil respiration (the sum of root and microbial contributions) is driven by surface soil moisture and large changes in the contribution of root respiration to total soil respiration occur seasonally; 2) episodic precipitation pulses derived from rainfall and fog drip drive large soil respiration responses; 3) microbial respiration responds more rapidly to episodic precipitation pulses than root respiration.
root and microbial contributions to total soil respiration (RS) respond differently in magnitude and timing to seasonal and episodically varying precipitation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the response of soil respiration (a large component of ecosystem carbon cycling) to seasonal and episodically varying precipitation patterns in a Mediterranean climate forest.
how the carbon cycle responds to changes in climate, specifically how changes in the timing, intensity and amount of moisture inputs influence carbon fluxes.
the role of soil moisture in regulating the exchange of carbon between plants and the atmosphere.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the seasonal and episodic patterns of SR in a Mediterranean pine forest are driven primarily by surface soil moisture and the contributions of root respiration.
the root and microbial contributions to SR respond differently in timing to seasonal and episodical moisture inputs.

the response of SR to moisture inputs in a Mediterranean type forest ecosystem is controlled by both seasonal and episodal moisture inputs, with microbial respiration responding rapidly to episodic inputs and root respiration responding to longer term seasonal changes in soil water.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
root and microbial contributions to SR respond differently to seasonal and episodically varying moisture inputs in a pine forest with Mediterranean type climate.
soil respiration in dry ecosystems responds rapidly to moisture inputs, but that root and microbial sources have different temporal dynamics and responses to changes in moisture.
the response of soil respiration (and its root and microbial components) to precipitation inputs is complex and highly variable in time and space.
The main takeaway from our work is that

root and microbial contributions to SR respond differently to both seasonal and short term precipitation inputs, with microbial respiration responding rapidly to water inputs, and root respiration responding to longer-term changes in soil moisture and plant growth.

both the magnitude and timing of soil respiration responses to precipitation pulses are driven by the source of the pulse (e.g. rain or fog drip) and the duration of the drought period preceding the pulse.

the response of soil respiration to episodic moisture pulses, which are becoming more frequent and intense due to climate change, can be very different than the response of SR to seasonal moisture inputs, which are typically represented in models.
